MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is coxa vara?"
- "A **neck–shaft angle below 120°**, with a Hilgenreiner–epiphyseal angle above 25°."
- "Three types: **congenital, developmental and acquired**."
- "The developmental type has a **vertical physis** and a **triangular fragment** in the inferior neck."

### Definition
The angle falls with growth, so "normal" depends on the age.
- **Coxa vara**: a neck–shaft angle reduced below normal (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- The working cut-off is **under 120°** (Handbook)
- **Coxa valga** is the opposite: an angle above normal

|---|---|
| Birth to 1 year | ≈**150°** |
| 5 years | ≈**140°** |
| Skeletal maturity | ≈**130°** (125–135°) |

- The angle falls as walking loads the hip
- Compare with the other hip in every child, not with an adult number

- The varus often sits **below the trochanters** (subtrochanteric)

### Acquired Coxa Vara
Here the neck bends because another disease weakened, broke or stopped it.

#### Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis
- SCFE is both cause and result of coxa vara
- A vertical physis turns weight into shear and invites a slip
- The slip leaves the head low and the shaft adducted
[[FIG: Fig 10.4 · 10.2
- Its old name is **adolescent coxa vara** → 09 Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

#### Sepsis, Perthes and Avascular Necrosis
- Septic arthritis damages the medial physis, so the neck stops growing
[[FIG: Fig 10.5 · 10.2
- Septic sequelae → 08 Late Sequelae of the Septic Hip
- Perthes and AVN after DDH treatment do the same → 05, 06, 03

#### Bone Disease and Dysplasia
- **Fibrous dysplasia** bends the femur into a **shepherd's crook**
[[FIG: Fig 10.6 · 10.2
- The lecture case was **bilateral and symmetric**
- Soft bone bends too: **rickets**, osteomalacia and osteogenesis imperfecta
- Skeletal dysplasias (spondyloepiphyseal, metaphyseal) give bilateral varus
[[FIG: Fig 10.7 · 10.2

#### Tumour and Trauma
- The commonest tumour is a **unicameral bone cyst** in the neck
[[FIG: Fig 10.8 · 10.2
- A **malunited or ununited** neck or subtrochanteric fracture tips the head down
[[FIG: Fig 10.9 · 10.2
- After a child's neck fracture, 100–110° does not remodel (Campbell)

The developmental type is the classic exam film: a toddler with a vertical physis and a small triangle under it.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is developmental coxa vara?"
- "A defect of **ossification in the inferomedial neck**, appearing after walking."
- "It shows the **Fairbank triangle**, a **vertical physis** and a **short neck**."
- "Boys and girls equally; bilateral in a third to half."

### Epidemiology
The child is usually a toddler or preschooler with a painless limp.

| Feature | Value |
|---|---|
| Incidence | ≈1 in **25,000** live births |
| Sex and side | boys = girls; right = left |
| Age | from walking age to **6 years** |
| Bilateral | **a third to half** (Miller) |
| Inheritance | familial cases; autosomal dominant reported |

### Pathogenesis
A weak neck meets the load of walking and bends.
- The cause is unknown, so it is also called **idiopathic**
- **Endochondral ossification** fails in the inferomedial neck
- The defect holds abnormal cartilage, like a second irregular physis (Campbell)
- The nearby metaphysis is osteoporotic, with thin trabeculae

#### Varus Collapse
- Walking increases the load on the weak neck
- The head sinks into **varus**, and the neck shortens
- The vertical physis turns weight into **shear** and medial compression
- Later the **greater trochanter** rises above the head

### Pathological Anatomy
Four findings together make the diagnosis.
[[FIG: Fig 10.10 · 10.3
| Finding | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Neck–shaft angle** reduced | varus |
| **Physis** very oblique or vertical | shear across the plate |
| **Fairbank triangle** | triangular metaphyseal fragment in the inferior neck |
| **Short neck** | not only varus; the neck has collapsed |

- Femoral **anteversion** is also reduced
- An atypical defect sits in the **upper** neck
[[FIG: Fig 10.11 · 10.3
- Neglected cases may form a **pseudarthrosis** of the neck

### Fairbank Triangle
This small triangle is the signature of the developmental type.
[[FIG: Fig 10.12 · 10.3
- A triangular fragment of metaphysis in the **inferomedial neck**
- It lies between the physis above and a second lucent line below
- Together the two lines look like an **inverted Y**
- The triangle is dystrophic bone, where the head collapses

PITFALL — which Fairbank triangle?
- Neck-of-femur questions list three triangles: Ward (osteoporosis), Babcock (TB) and Fairbank
- Say → "**Fairbank triangle = coxa vara**: the inferomedial metaphyseal fragment of developmental coxa vara"

MEMORY HOOK — the inverted Y
- The neck of developmental coxa vara writes a small upside-down Y: the physis and the second line, with the Fairbank triangle sitting between its legs.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how does coxa vara present?"
- "A **painless limp**: Trendelenburg if unilateral, **waddling** if bilateral."
- "A **high greater trochanter**, a short leg and limited abduction."
- "Bilateral cases mimic DDH, but **rotation is limited**."

### Symptoms and Gait
A high trochanter slackens the abductors, and the gait shows it.
- Usually **painless**
- **Unilateral**: Trendelenburg gait and a short leg
- **Bilateral**: **waddling gait** and excessive lumbar lordosis
- Older patients may complain of hip pain

### Signs
Each sign comes from the low head and the high trochanter.

| Sign | Why |
|---|---|
| **High greater trochanter** | above the line of the head |
| Positive **Trendelenburg test** | short abductor lever, weak abductors |
| **Leg length discrepancy** | supratrochanteric; shown by the Klisic test |
| Limited **passive abduction** | superior neck hits the acetabular rim early |
| Limited **active abduction** | weak abductors |

- Hip motion is often restricted in all planes, without tenderness

### Differential Diagnosis From DDH
Bilateral coxa vara waddles like bilateral DDH; rotation separates them.

| | Coxa vara | DDH |
|---|---|---|
| Gait if bilateral | waddling | waddling |
| Rotation | **limited** | **excessive** |
| Head | in the acetabulum | out of the acetabulum |

PITFALL — the waddling toddler
- A waddling toddler is not always DDH; coxa vara waddles too
- Say → "**check rotation, then an AP pelvis: head in the socket, vertical physis = coxa vara**"

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you measure coxa vara?"
- "**Neck–shaft angle**, but the short neck is hard to measure."
- "So the **Hilgenreiner–epiphyseal angle**: normal under 25°, coxa vara 40–70°."
- "Under 45° resolves, 45–60° is watched, over **60°** progresses."

### Radiographic Views
One view is enough for the developmental type.
- **Developmental**: one **AP pelvis** is usually enough (Handbook)
- **Acquired**: AP and **frog-lateral**, to see the underlying disease
- MRI shows a widened, irregular physis; it is rarely needed

### The Three Angles
Each angle uses a different line, and only one predicts the future.
[[FIG: Fig 10.13 · 10.5

| Angle | Lines | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Neck–shaft angle** | neck axis vs shaft axis | definition; hard in a short neck |
| **Head–shaft angle** | perpendicular to the epiphysis base vs shaft axis | alternative |
| **Hilgenreiner–epiphyseal (HE) angle** | Hilgenreiner line vs physis line | **prognosis and treatment** |

#### Limits of the Neck–Shaft Angle
- The neck axis joins the midpoints of the neck
- In severe coxa vara the neck is too short to draw an axis
- In SCFE the neck–shaft angle stays normal, yet the hip is in varus

### Hilgenreiner–Epiphyseal Angle
This is the angle the examiner wants you to draw.
[[FIG: Fig 10.14 · 10.5
- Draw **Hilgenreiner line** through both triradiate cartilages
- Draw the **physis line** along the full length of the physis
- Measure the angle between them
[[FIG: Fig 10.15 · 10.5
- Normal is under **25°**, about **16°** on average (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Coxa vara usually measures **40–70°**

### Weinstein Thresholds
The HE angle predicts which hips correct and which progress.
[[FIG: Fig 10.16 · 10.5

| HE angle | Course | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **< 45°** | corrects spontaneously | observe |
| **45–60°** | uncertain | watch closely; operate if progressing |
| **> 60°** | progresses | **valgus osteotomy** |

- These thresholds come from Weinstein's series (Campbell, Miller)
- The lecture's child at ≈45° was observed
[[FIG: Fig 10.17 · 10.5
- The second child, far above 60°, needed surgery
[[FIG: Fig 10.18 · 10.5

MEMORY HOOK — 45 and 60
- Under 45 the hip heals itself; over 60 it needs the saw; between them it needs a calendar.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what if you leave it?"
- "The varus progresses; shear causes a **stress fracture**, then **non-union**."
- "The trochanter rises above the head, so the **abductors fail**."
- "Without normal load the acetabulum grows **dysplastic**, then arthritic."

### Progression of the Neck
- A smaller angle means more **shear** across the neck
- Shear causes a stress fracture, then **non-union** and more varus
[[FIG: Fig 10.19 · 10.6
- In adults the trochanter may lie centimetres above the head (Campbell)

### Effect on the Acetabulum
- The acetabulum grows only around a loaded head
- Abductor insufficiency removes that normal load
- The result is **acetabular dysplasia**, then osteoarthritis

### Time Window
- After **8 years** the chance of a normally working hip falls fast (Campbell)

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you treat developmental coxa vara?"
- "HE under 45°: observe. 45–60°: watch. Over **60°**, or neck–shaft **110° or less**: operate."
- "**Subtrochanteric valgus osteotomy**, overcorrected, with **lateral translation** of the distal fragment."
- "Aim for HE under 40° and neck–shaft over 120°; follow to maturity for **recurrence**."

### Aims of Treatment
Treatment restores mechanics, not just the angle.
- Prevent **secondary deformity** of the acetabulum
- Restore normal mechanics, so the acetabulum grows normally
- Correct the limp and the **leg length discrepancy**
- Correct **abductor insufficiency**

### Indications
Most indications are numbers; the rest are symptoms.

| Indication for surgery | Source |
|---|---|
| HE angle **> 60°** | Campbell, Miller |
| HE angle 45–60° that is **progressing** or symptomatic | lecture, Orthobullets |
| Neck–shaft angle **≤ 110°** | Campbell |
| Progression, pain or leg length discrepancy | Campbell |

#### The Handbook Severity Scale
| Grade | Neck–shaft | HE angle | Handbook plan |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mild | 110–120° | 25–45° | observe |
| Moderate | 100–110° | 45–60° | physiotherapy for the abductors |
| Severe | < 100° | > 60° | valgus osteotomy |

PITFALL — operate under 100° or at 110°?
- The Handbook operates under 100°; Campbell, Miller and Orthobullets at 110° or less
- Say → "**HE over 60°, or neck–shaft 110° or less, or progression: valgus osteotomy**"

### Valgus Osteotomy
The standard operation turns the physis horizontal, so shear becomes compression.
- Valgus osteotomy is the treatment of choice (Campbell)
- **Greater trochanteric epiphysiodesis** alone was tried and is ineffective (Prof Abdel-Ghani)

#### Choice of Osteotomy
| Osteotomy | Level and shape | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Pauwels Y-shaped** | intertrochanteric; lateral wedge closed, medial limb opened | shaft ends **medial** |
| Langenskiöld | intertrochanteric valgus | little correction of retroversion |
| **Borden** | subtrochanteric, just below the lesser trochanter | end-to-side valgization |

- The lecture names **Pauwels** as the most important
[[FIG: Fig 10.20 · 10.7
- Its drawback: it **medializes** the distal fragment (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- A valgus osteotomy needs **lateralization** of the distal fragment instead
- Campbell prefers a **subtrochanteric** osteotomy at the lesser trochanter
[[FIG: Fig 10.21 · 10.7

#### Timing
- There is no fixed age; the lecture operated at 4, 5 and 7 years
[[FIG: Fig 10.22 · 10.7
- Campbell delays to **4–5 years**, so fixation is easier

#### Technique
- First an **adductor tenotomy** through a small medial incision
- Lateral approach to the proximal femur
- Fix the proximal fragment below the trochanteric apophysis

#### Correction and Fixation
- Plan the correction: HE angle minus the normal 16°
[[FIG: Fig 10.23 · 10.7
- Transverse osteotomy at the level of the **lesser trochanter**, with a small lateral wedge
- Overcorrect the neck–shaft angle to **140–150°** (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 10.24 · 10.7
- Derotate if the neck is retroverted
- Fix with a blade plate or a screw and side plate
[[FIG: Fig 10.25 · 10.7
- One-and-a-half **spica** until union, about 8–12 weeks

#### Fixation Points From the Lecture
- A **smooth wire** may cross the physis to stop it slipping during correction
[[FIG: Fig 10.26 · 10.7
- **Never a screw** across the physis
[[FIG: Fig 10.27 · 10.7
- A lag screw left across the physis later shortened this neck
[[FIG: Fig 10.28 · 10.7
- If the distal fragment will not reduce, **shorten** the shaft

#### Prerequisite: Adduction
- The hip must **adduct** before surgery
- Valgus without adduction range leaves a fixed **abduction deformity**
- After the osteotomy the hip must reach **neutral**
- Valgus lowers the trochanter and tightens the abductors

#### Abductor Release
- If neutral is not reached, the **abductors** are too tight
- Slide their origin down by taking **1–2 cm of iliac crest**, then close (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- This lowers the abductors without cutting them

PFFD is the congenital end of the spectrum: the femur itself is short and its top is missing.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is PFFD?"
- "A congenital defect of the **proximal femur**: shortening, varus and an unstable hip."
- "**Aitken A–D** by head, acetabulum and femoral segment."
- "Treatment rests on **hip stability** and **percentage shortening**."

### Definition and Epidemiology
The spectrum runs from a slightly short femur to near absence.
[[FIG: Fig 10.49 · 10.9
- A congenital **partial defect** of the proximal femur
- With a variably **unstable hip** and marked shortening
- Incidence ≈**1 in 50,000** births
- Linked to **thalidomide** exposure (Handbook) and maternal diabetes (Campbell)
- Bilateral in about **20%** (Handbook)

#### Associated Anomalies
- **Fibular hemimelia**: the commonest, in about half (Miller)
- Absent **cruciate ligaments** of the knee
- Clubfoot, tarsal coalition, cardiac and spinal anomalies
[[FIG: Fig 10.50 · 10.9

### Clinical Features
The thigh is short, bulky and held in a typical attitude.
[[FIG: Fig 10.51 · 10.9
- Short **bulky thigh**, flexed, abducted and externally rotated (Miller)
- Severe leg length discrepancy
- Hip and knee **flexion contractures**, genu valgum
- The percentage of shortening stays **constant** during growth

### Aitken Classification
Aitken grades the head, the acetabulum and the femoral segment.
[[FIG: Fig 10.52 · 10.9

| Class | Femoral head | Acetabulum | Femoral segment | Hip |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | present | normal | short; neck ossifies late, subtrochanteric varus | stable |
| **B** | present | adequate or moderately dysplastic | short; **no bony connection** to the head | stable |
| **C** | absent or an ossicle | **severely dysplastic** | short, tapered | unstable |
| **D** | absent | **absent** | short, deformed; obturator foramen enlarged | unstable |

- Class D is often **bilateral**
[[FIG: Fig 10.53 · 10.9
- The ossific head may appear late; arthrography or MRI shows the cartilage
[[FIG: Fig 10.54 · 10.9

MEMORY HOOK — A to D, losing parts
- Aitken loses one part per letter: A has all parts but a crooked neck, B loses the neck bridge, C loses the head, D loses the socket too.

### Paley Classification
Paley sorts congenital femoral deficiency by what can be rebuilt.
[[FIG: Fig 10.55 · 10.9
- **Type 1**: intact femur; 1a normal and 1b **delayed** ossification of the neck
- **Type 2**: mobile **pseudarthrosis** between head and shaft
- **Type 3**: deficient femoral **shaft**; in 3c the femur is absent
- **Type 4**: the deficiency is distal

#### Treatment by Paley Type
- Type 1: **SUPERhip** hip reconstruction first, then lengthening
- Types 2 and 3: best suited to **rotationplasty** (Brown or Paley–Brown)

### Principles of Management
Two facts decide the plan: is the hip stable, and how short will the femur be?
[[FIG: Fig 10.56 · 10.9
- Treatment is individual; often no surgery is needed
- **Bilateral** PFFD is treated without surgery; extension prostheses if wanted
- A prosthesis around the foot equalizes length, often as a temporary step
[[FIG: Fig 10.57 · 10.9

| Hip | Predicted length | Plan |
|---|---|---|
| Stable | **> 50%** of the other side | lengthening ± contralateral epiphysiodesis |
| Stable | **< 50%** | knee fusion + Syme, or knee fusion + **rotationplasty** |
| Unstable | any | femoropelvic fusion + Syme or rotationplasty |

#### Lengthening
- Only if the femur is over **50%** of predicted length (Campbell)
- Or the projected shortening is under **20 cm**
- One congenital bone lengthens **10–12 cm** at most
- Stages at 4–5 years, 8–9 years and adolescence
- Correct coxa vara to 120° and dysplasia first, or the hip subluxates

#### Knee Fusion and Foot Amputation
- Fuse the knee, so tibia and femur act as one long thigh
[[FIG: Fig 10.58 · 10.9
- Then a **Syme** or Boyd amputation
- The child walks like an above-knee amputee with a prosthesis
- Time epiphysiodesis so the prosthetic knee matches the other knee

### Van Nes Rotationplasty
The ankle becomes the knee.
[[FIG: Fig 10.59 · 10.9
- Fuse the knee and rotate the leg **180°** externally
- Ankle **plantarflexion** becomes knee extension
- Ankle **dorsiflexion** becomes knee flexion
- The child wears a **below-knee** prosthesis
[[FIG: Fig 10.60 · 10.9

#### Conditions and Problems
- Needs a reasonably **stable hip**
- Needs an ankle arc of at least **90°** (Campbell)
- Derotation occurs in up to **50%** of young children
- The backward foot may disturb the family; show them another patient

PITFALL — rotationplasty or amputation?
- Rotationplasty needs a good ankle, but many PFFD children have fibular hemimelia
- Say → "**stable hip, under 50% length and a mobile ankle: rotationplasty; poor ankle: knee fusion and Syme**"

### Unstable Hip
When there is no head or no socket, the knee becomes the hip.
- **Steel iliofemoral fusion**: the femoral remnant is fused to the pelvis
[[FIG: Fig 10.61 · 10.9
- A **Chiari** osteotomy makes a bed for the remnant
- The femur is fused at **90°** flexion, so knee extension becomes hip flexion
- **Brown**: rotate the limb 180° and fuse the distal femur to the pelvis
[[FIG: Fig 10.62 · 10.9
- Then the knee works as a hip and the ankle as a knee
